Le bébé est minuscule, aussi petit qu’un: The baby is tiny, as small as a doll. Her mother, Kadiatou Bah, proudly carries her daughter through the living room of the La Traverse shelter. “She was born nine days ago!” says Kisha Estimée, the shelter’s director. “She saw her being born,” adds the new mother, an asylum seeker from Guinea who has lived for months in the transition house in Montréal-Nord.
Alors que l’itinérance guette les demand: As homelessness looms over asylum seekers, citizen-led initiatives are emerging to keep exorbitant housing prices from making an already fragile population even more precarious. According to a report published in September 2023 in Montréal, one in 10 people experiencing homelessness is an asylum seeker.
Le visage radieux, mais fatigué de la je: The young mother’s radiant but tired face hides a harsher reality. “I almost killed myself after I arrived in Canada,” Kadiatou says bluntly. She had to leave behind her first daughter, who was two years old at the time and whom she had to hide before leaving because of threats.
Pour Kadiatou, la maison d’hébergement L: For Kadiatou, the La Traverse shelter has been a lifeline. She didn’t know anyone in Montréal. Thinking about the hard road that brought her to Canada, about her first child and the difficulties of family reunification, not to mention the economic reality and the spectre of ending up on the street, leaves her completely disoriented.
Kadiatou est bien tombée : au centre d’h: Kadiatou landed in a good place: at the La Traverse shelter, where she has been living for four months, she has her own room because she has a newborn. Here, Kisha Estimée makes the decisions. While residents generally have three months to find permanent housing, she handles things case by case.
« C’est une très bonne personne et elle: “She is a very good person and she really deserves a lot of help, given her strength and courage,” says the woman who accompanied the mother through her delivery.
Les centres d’hébergement gérés par Québ: Shelters run by Quebec or Ottawa have a cut-off date by which asylum seekers must leave. The time limit is generally two to three weeks. After that, asylum seekers have to fend for themselves.
La cuisine sent bon l’odeur riche de la: The kitchen smells rich with the aroma of soup joumou, a classic of Haitian cuisine. A woman keeps an eye on the pot while doing the dishes. Here, the 27 people who live at the shelter become roommates and are responsible for keeping the place in good order.
« Je demande que tout le monde mette la: “I ask that everyone pitch in. Clean to keep things tidy and not break anything, because I’m the one who buys them, otherwise we have to wait for donations,” says Kisha Estimée, noting that people are making an effort.
Au moment de notre visite, les résidents: At the time of our visit, the residents of La Traverse come from Mexico, Senegal, the Congo (DRC), Haiti, Brazil, Kenya, Burkina Faso and Guinea.
« Aider, c’est ma passion. Je suis née i: “Helping is my passion. I was born here, I’m a Canadian of Haitian origin,” says the woman whose parents arrived from Haiti in 1961, the year François Duvalier became “president for life” by imposing his dictatorship.
Les parents de Kisha Estimée s’impliquen: Kisha Estimée’s parents got involved as soon as they arrived in Quebec, and her father even took his daughter to Haiti to do humanitarian work. She believes her upbringing had a great influence on the creation of the shelter.
Malgré toutes les bonnes volontés, la di: Despite all the goodwill, finding funding for this type of project is a challenge. While Quebec began demanding just days ago that Ottawa reimburse $1 billion to offset the expenses incurred to serve asylum seekers, small organizations suffer from chronic underfunding.
« Ce n’est pas parce que les grands orga: “Just because the big organizations receive money doesn’t mean it gets to us or that we’ll be able to survive. They need to come and give [the funding] to us directly,” says Kisha Estimée as she picks up a few toys in the living room of the La Traverse transition shelter, which she founded on her own almost four years ago. Besides her house, there are two other shelters of the same type in Montréal: Le Pont and Foyer du Monde. Together, these three organizations form an ad hoc coalition called the Regroupement des organismes en hébergement pour personnes migrantes (ROHMI).
Cependant, le ministère de l’Immigration: However, Quebec’s Ministry of Immigration “does not fund any personal initiative for housing immigrants or asylum seekers,” says a ministry spokesperson.
Au Québec, c’est le Programme régional d: In Quebec, it is the Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile (PRAIDA), under the Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux (MSSS), that funds temporary housing for asylum seekers.
Depuis le début de ses opérations, Mme E: Since the start of her operations, Ms. Estimée has been running on donations. Recent assistance from the Foundation of Greater Montréal granted her $195,000 over three years to pay the rent.
Elle doit cependant assumer les frais si: She must, however, cover the costs if someone is in need. “If the person can’t pay, I’ll try to find a solution. I’ll keep them here because I can’t leave them on the street.”
Kadiatou corrobore ses dires, elle qui a: Kadiatou confirms what she says, having seen over the past four months the work and effort put in at La Traverse. “I see her, Kisha; she sometimes pays out of her own pocket to treat us.”
Elle sait qu’elle bénéficie d’une except: She knows she is benefiting from an exception, because her situation is complex. The young mother wants to bring her eldest daughter, who remained back home, and would like to find a job in an NGO, as she holds a degree in organizational sociology.

Située dans le quartier populaire et bra: Located in the working-class and trendy East Vancouver neighbourhood in British Columbia, the Kinbrace shelter goes unnoticed. Its founder is sitting in the bright living room when he welcomes us, surrounded by toys. In the big kitchen, people are coming and going.
Plusieurs employés s'affairent à régler: Several employees are busy sorting out files for the tenants of the Kinbrace apartments. They provide special follow-up and support to all residents.Photo: Anais Elboujdaini
« À l’époque, nous voulions répondre aux: “Back then, we wanted to respond to the pressing needs of our community. The model we chose was to better understand and support people by living with them,” says Loren Balisky. The co-founder of Kinbrace, which now has nine housing units, lived for 19 years in one of the units with his wife and their children, surrounded by asylum seekers.
Ils ont d’abord acquis une grande maison: They first acquired a large house with seven self-contained units in the building. It had been renovated in the late 1980s. After several years, they bought the house next door.
L’idée est simple : deux familles canadi: The idea is simple: two Canadian families live in the same apartment complex as six asylum-seeker families. “It’s a very transformative way of being together and of walking alongside people who are experiencing forced displacement,” says the man who started the project in collaboration with his church in 1998.
Aujourd’hui, Kinbrace bénéficie du souti: Today, Kinbrace receives financial support from a multitude of non-profit organizations and charities. The shelter also receives donations from the Vancouver credit union and from individuals, in addition to proceeds from several fundraisers. There are not many initiatives like it in the western province.
Loren Balisky est cofondateur de l'initi: Loren Balisky is the co-founder of the Kinbrace initiative, which for 25 years has welcomed asylum seekers to help them transition into the community.Photo: Anais Elboujdaini
Des milliers de kilomètres les séparent,: Thousands of kilometres separate them, but the projects of Loren Balisky and Kisha Estimée stem from the same kind of personal initiative.
Les réalités sont peut-être différentes: The realities may be different – British Columbia took in 7,695 asylum seekers last year, while Quebec received 65,570 over the same period – but for both founders, people are at the heart of what they do.
« J’ai toujours aimé aider les gens », r: “I’ve always loved helping people,” says Kisha Estimée in Montréal, while Mr. Balisky is pleased that in 25 years, Kinbrace has become “like a little village.”
« Quand il s’agit de relations et que ce: “When it’s about relationships and not just a service, you can no longer lock people or a population into stereotypes,” he says.

Les difficultés sont nombreuses, et le c: The challenges are many, and the picture gradually emerges: people need psychological follow-up, the money to keep the shelter running barely suffices, and demand keeps growing.
Les délais d’attente sont variables, car: Wait times vary, because she also considers the person’s needs, their situation and their ability to fit in with the rest of the household. Kisha Estimée also sees more and more people who need psychological support… and even psychiatric care.
Avec la difficulté de trouver un logemen: With the difficulty of finding affordable housing, a trend is emerging: asylum seekers who, a few years ago, moved into the Vancouver neighbourhood now have to find housing much farther out in the suburbs. Previously, a one-bedroom apartment in the neighbourhood cost $600 a month. Today, it is $2,500 a month.
Une situation que déplore M. Balisky, pu: Mr. Balisky laments the situation, since it weakens the model he set up and the importance of keeping asylum seekers close to their first place of welcome. “We became an anchor point where people who stayed with us for a few months would then move into the neighbourhood. We’d see each other on the streets and they would come over from time to time for dinner at the weekly communal meal we share.”
Chez Kinbrace, le fondateur croit qu’il: At Kinbrace, the founder believes temporary transitional housing needs to be built for asylum seekers, because they are vulnerable. “I haven’t done in-depth research, but the success of the asylum seekers who come through here seems directly linked to how long they were able to stay [in our facility] to get back on their feet.”
Kadiatou change la couche de sa petite d: Kadiatou changes her little girl’s diaper in a room she has occupied since September. Kisha Estimée made an exception in light of the situation Kadiatou was going through. When asked the baby’s name, everyone shares the same knowing smile.

Ces moments donnent à celle qu’on surnom: These moments give the woman nicknamed the “Mother Teresa of Montréal-Nord” the strength to keep running her shelter.
« C’est juste des étoiles dans les yeux,: “It’s just stars in my eyes, wonders for four years. I’ve seen families grow here, I had a mom with triplets. Listen, there are a lot of things here that stay with me,” she says, cradling the baby who bears her name.
À Vancouver, Loren Balisky nous fait fai: In Vancouver, Loren Balisky gives us a tour of the property. In the kitchen, a young boy runs among the staff. Hens escape from their pen in the backyard, and he bursts out laughing. The house, which has seen hundreds of families pass through, is a stronghold where bonds are formed, sometimes for life.

« Nous n’avons pas de limites pour que l: “We don’t set limits on when people have to leave,” he says, aware of the support residents receive over the weeks.
« Nous aidons de 40 à 50 personnes par a: “We help 40 to 50 people a year move from homelessness to permanent housing. The profile of asylum seekers is varied. We house families, single people, single mothers and seniors,” says Mr. Balisky.

Cette tendance inquiète M. Balisky, qui: This trend worries Mr. Balisky, who fears for the mental health of asylum seekers who use these kinds of places.
« Je l’entends dire par les demandeurs d: “I hear it from asylum seekers who have been in these shelters – it’s very traumatic for them. In Vancouver, they are often in the Downtown Eastside. I obviously support all of that, but no one is planning for what’s coming. It’s like closing your eyes, guessing how many people will arrive and then responding in a rush,” he says.
Dans la salle commune de Kinbrace, qui d: In Kinbrace’s common room, which overlooks the backyard, an Afghan couple communicates laboriously with a shelter employee. The couple introduces themselves to us, nodding.
M. Balisky secoue la sienne, avant d’exp: Mr. Balisky shakes his head, then explains, with a hint of distress, that their refugee status claim is complex. He adds that they nevertheless have the support of some staff during the day: “I always wonder how many people on their own are denied refugee status because of simple mistakes in this bureaucratic process.”
« Si nous étions vraiment progressistes: “If we were truly progressive as a country [...] we would abolish the barriers and make it possible for asylum seekers to integrate quickly,” he laments, having seen the complexity of the immigration system for 25 years.

M<sup>me</sup> Estimée lui a donné sa pr: M<sup>me</sup> Estimée gave him his first chance by offering him work as a security guard for the shelter. She was able to do so because she runs her project entirely on her own and is free to open her door to whomever she chooses.
« Mais ce n’est pas gratuit, parce que m: “But it’s not free, because I built this without any grants. That means when people are on social assistance, they’re able to pay me a small amount,” explains M<sup>me</sup> Estimée. A family on social assistance pays $590 a month.
« Il y a toujours une file devant ma por: “There’s always a line at my door. Three weeks ago, it was an endless line, because PRAIDA sends them to me.
